newsitem.title: PERU: Peru lawmakers demand Congress probe of crisis.
newsitem.headline: Peru lawmakers demand Congress probe of crisis.

text.p: Opposition lawmakers are calling for a congressional investigation into the failure by Peru's security forces to foil the takeover of the Japanese ambassador's Lima home by Marxist rebels 2 1/2 months ago.
"We are going to propose an exhaustive investigation," Congressman Fernando Olivera of the Independent Moralizing Front (FIM) party told local television late on Tuesday.

Congress is dominated by President Alberto Fujimori's Change 90-New Majority party. But even opposition lawmakers had not called for a probe before because "we felt it prudent to maintain a silence until the hostage crisis ended," Olivera said.

That changed this week when Fujimori admitted that Peru's intelligence service (SIN) and police knew weeks before the Dec. 17 takeover that Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels planned a hostage-taking in Lima.

Fujimori said the SIN informed police the MRTA was shipping arms and combatants to Lima from Peru's central jungle and police high command ordered preventive steps but, "apparently, adequate measures were not taken."

A band of heavily-armed MRTA guerrillas stormed the diplomatic compound and seized hundreds of VIP cocktail party guests. All but 72 men have been released in what has become Latin America's longest hostage siege.

The president blamed police and "some officials" for failing to prevent the crisis, adding that a government probe was under way and some authorities may be punished. But some opposition lawmakers want Congress to investigate.
"This is a subject that, in the proper moment, must be investigated in depth by a congressional commission," said Jorge del Castillo of the Aprista party.

Some said Interior Minister Juan Briones should be hauled before Congress to explain what went wrong. Others said further explanations are needed as Fujimori now has retreated from initial statements that the powerful SIN may also be at fault.

"President Fujimori has changed from one day to the next," said lawmaker Ernesto Gamarra. "He had signalled there was responsibility on the part of the National Intelligence Service and now the responsibility is attributed to lower levels within the police."

But pro-government lawmakers and some independents said it is not the right time to try to affix blame because the crisis continues. On Wednesday, the mostly middle-aged hostages began their 71st day in captivity at the residence with no early end in sight to their ordeal.
"While we have this front open at the Japanese embassy, it is better to maintain moderation," Enrique Chirinos Soto of the Renovation party said.

"This is not the right time to determine responsibility," added Ricardo Marcenaro of Change 90-New Majority. "We have to wait until this process is ended and at that moment determine exactly who are responsible."
